docs.title: pysoarm
docs.text:
A lean, hardware-level Python API for the SO-100 / SO-101 robot arm: six Feetech STS3215 serial-bus servos on a single 1 Mbaud TTL bus.

pysoarm talks to the bus directly and stops there — no datasets, no policies, no training stack. The ergonomics follow pylibfranka / pyAgxArm (connect() → read_once() → write_goal() / control loop) within what position-servo hardware can actually do.

Version 0.1.1

Transport (scs and the optional rustypot backend), the motor-side calibration flow, safety, trajectories, Cartesian kinematics, SOArm (follower and read-only leader), diagnostics (health(), doctor --stress), the ArmBridge/ROS 2 adapter and the CLI are implemented. What is not here is by design: teleoperation, dataset recording and policies (ADR 0001). See CHANGELOG.md for the full list.

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
user code / policy / script
                   │
        ┌──────────▼───────────┐
        │        SOArm         │  arm.py       device lifetime, torque, control loop
        └──────────┬───────────┘
     ┌─────────────┼──────────────┬─────────────────┐
     ▼             ▼              ▼                 ▼
 safety.py    trajectory.py  calibration.py   kinematics/
 (guards)     (interpolators) (deg ↔ ticks)   (optional FK/IK)
     └─────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────┘
                   │  raw ticks, sync transactions
        ┌──────────▼───────────┐
        │         Bus          │  bus/base.py  Protocol — the only I/O boundary
        └──────────┬───────────┘
        ┌──────────┼───────────┐
        ▼          ▼           ▼
     scs.py   rustypot.py   fake.py
   (pyserial)  (optional)   (tests/dev)

make_bus(port, ids, backend="scs" | "rustypot" | "auto") picks one; auto prefers rustypot when it is importable. scs is the default so behaviour does not depend on what happens to be installed (2.8 ms per control step vs 1.4 ms).

Rule: nothing above bus/ may import serial or rustypot; nothing below bus/ may know about degrees, calibration or limits. That boundary is what makes the whole control path testable on a laptop. What belongs inside this boundary — and what is deliberately left to the application layer — is decided in ADR 0001.

docs.title: Control step
docs.text:
read_once():   sync_read  Present_Position (+1 health register/tick)  1.0-2.2 ms
               → ArmState (immutable)
guards:        validate → soft limits → per-step clip → thermal/supply
write_goal():  sync_write Goal_Position (one broadcast frame)          ~0.26 ms
               → returns the goal actually sent

Timing is owned by SOArm.run_control_loop, never by the trajectory: absolute-deadline scheduling on a monotonic clock, overruns counted and reported (not silently absorbed).

docs.title: Error model
docs.text:
Situation Exception Arm state afterwards port busy / cannot open BusConnectionError unchanged, no torque change reply missing after retries CommunicationError goal held, watchdog counts up watchdog trips WatchdogTimeout torque off goal would be unsafe SafetyViolation or clamped goal last safe goal bad configuration/calibration ConfigurationError / CalibrationError no I/O performed

stop() is idempotent and safe from a signal handler and from finally; leaving torque enabled after an exception is treated as a bug (see SECURITY.md).

docs.title: Hardware notes
docs.text: Everything below was measured on a real SO-101 follower (six STS3215 servos, CH343 USB-CDC adapter, 1 Mbaud, 12 V supply).

docs.title: Capability matrix
docs.text: Franka (libfranka) SO-101 (STS3215) Loop rate 1 kHz, hard real-time 200–500 Hz, soft real-time (USB CDC) Command torque τ, q/dq, Cartesian impedance Goal_Position (internal PID); velocity / pwm / step modes available Feedback q, dq, τ, external wrench, pose q (4096 ticks/turn), speed, current/load estimate, voltage, temperature Force control yes no — coarse stall/collision detection from current only Kinematics bundled model bring your own URDF Safety hard limits, watchdog you implement it (safety.py)

docs.title: Measured timings
docs.text:
Measured on the reference arm, both backends:

Operation scs (pure Python) rustypot (optional extra) single register read 0.36 ms — sync_read, 6 joints 2.18 ms 0.98 ms sync_write, 6 goals 0.26 ms 0.26 ms read + write (one control step) 2.79 ms 1.44 ms 200 Hz loop, 1 s 200 ticks, 3–6 overruns 200 ticks, 0 overruns

scs is the default: one small dependency (pyserial), no compiled extension. Install pysoarm[rustypot] and pass backend="rustypot" (or --backend rustypot) to halve the read cost — the only real performance lever on this hardware.

docs.title: Wire protocol
docs.text:
request   FF FF  ID  LEN  INSTR  [PARAMS...]  CHECKSUM
response  FF FF  ID  LEN  ERROR  [DATA...]    CHECKSUM
  • LEN = len(PARAMS) + 2 — a two-byte READ therefore uses LEN = 4;
  • CHECKSUM = ~(ID + LEN + INSTR + PARAMS...) & 0xFF;
  • broadcast id 0xFE; SYNC_WRITE = 0x83;
  • positions are sign-magnitude (bit 15), not two's complement;
  • the bus is half-duplex: pipelining six READ requests before reading any reply corrupts the stream (observed on hardware), so reads are sequential. SYNC_WRITE is safe to broadcast because the host is the only transmitter.

docs.text: Register Addr Size Encoding Torque_Enable 40 1 unsigned Goal_Position 42 2 sign-magnitude (15) Present_Position 56 2 sign-magnitude (15) Present_Speed 58 2 sign-magnitude (15) Present_Load 60 2 sign-magnitude (10) Present_Voltage 62 1 0.1 V/LSB Present_Temperature 63 1 °C Present_Current 69 2 unsigned Operating_Mode 33 1 0 position / 1 velocity / 2 pwm / 3 step Homing_Offset 31 2 sign-magnitude (11) Min/Max_Position_Limit 9 / 11 2 unsigned P/I/D_Coefficient 21 / 23 / 22 1 unsigned Acceleration / Maximum_Acceleration 41 / 85 1 unsigned Return_Delay_Time 7 1 unsigned Phase 18 1 unsigned (bit 4 must be clear) Max_Torque_Limit / Protection_Current / Overload_Torque 16 / 28 / 36 2/2/1 gripper caps

docs.title: Known traps
docs.text:
• Exclusive port. Two processes on one tty → Device or resource busy. stop() a LeRobot run properly with Ctrl+C; a suspended (Ctrl+Z) process keeps the port.
  • ModemManager probes /dev/ttyACM* on hotplug and can win the race. sudo systemctl disable --now ModemManager.
  • tty numbering is not stable — use the packaged udev rule to get /dev/so101_follower.
  • Single-turn encoders: wrist_roll wraps at 0/4095; there is no multi-turn count.
  • Torque off means limp: read positions before enabling torque, and always command the measured position first.
  • Thermals: sustained motion pushes the servos past 60 °C and the firmware derates.

Short, dated records of decisions that are expensive to reverse. Each ADR states the context, the decision, and the consequences — including what we deliberately give up.

ADR Title Status 0001 Scope: pysoarm is a device-layer SDK Accepted

docs.title: ADR 0001 — Scope: pysoarm is a device-layer SDK
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Deciders: jw
  • Related: SECURITY.md (repo root), Architecture, Hardware notes

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The SO-100/SO-101 stack already has an application layer: LeRobot provides teleoperation, dataset recording (v3.0 format, video encoding, Hub upload), replay, policies and training. What it does not provide is a small, dependency-light, typesafe driver for the bus that a user can build on without importing torch.

Every new capability added to a library is a long-term maintenance contract. Recording in particular implies: camera capture, video encoding (NVENC/VAAPI/SVT-AV1 fallbacks), a parquet/JSONL dataset schema owned by another project, statistics computation, resumable episodes and Hub upload. That contract is versioned by upstream, not by us.

We therefore need an explicit rule for what belongs in pysoarm, to keep scope creep and dependency growth in check.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A feature belongs in pysoarm if, and only if, it is a physical fact of a single device: a register address, an encoder scale, a calibration constant, a limit, a timing constraint, a status bit. Multi-device coordination, data formats and learning stacks stay outside.

Function Classification Where it lives Register access, sync read/write, torque enable device fact pysoarm/bus/ Calibration (homing offset, ranges, ticks ↔ degrees) device fact — defines the unit pysoarm/calibration.py Limits, per-step clipping, thermal/supply guards, watchdog device fact pysoarm/safety.py Joint-space trajectory interpolation single-device timing pysoarm/trajectory.py State snapshots device fact pysoarm/state.py FK/IK, Cartesian goals model fact, needs a third-party solver pysoarm/kinematics/ (optional extra) Teleoperation (leader → follower, input events) two devices + an interaction policy user code, or LeRobot Dataset recording (cameras, video, parquet, Hub) data-format contract + codecs LeRobot Policies / training / inference learning stack LeRobot

Teleoperation is deliberately a ~10-line user program, because it is a policy:

follower.write_goal(leader.read_once().q_deg)

Putting that in the SDK would bake a specific master/slave topology, joint order and gripper convention into the library, and force a background-thread architecture on the synchronous read_once() / run_control_loop() API.

Replay is supported as a primitive, not a format: ResampledTrajectory replays any (t, q) table, and examples/replay_trajectory.py shows it. No dataset schema is assumed.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive

  • Runtime dependencies stay at pyserial (+ optional rustypot); the wheel stays tiny and installs anywhere, including machines that cannot build or run torch.
  • import pysoarm needs no camera, no codec, no network, no GPU.
  • The whole control path is testable on a laptop with FakeBus; only the transport needs hardware.
  • No version coupling to an external dataset schema.

Negative / accepted costs

  • Users who want a one-command "record an episode" must use LeRobot (or ~50 lines of their own code). We accept the seam.
  • Two processes must not hold the serial port at the same time: LeRobot recording and a pysoarm script cannot run concurrently on the same arm. Documented as a known trap.
  • If we ever add recording, it starts as a separate package/adapter, not as a new module in the core import path.

Explicit non-goals

  1. Teleoperation, master/slave modes, input devices.
  2. Dataset recording, video encoding, dataset schema compatibility, Hub upload.
  3. Policy inference, training, RL environments.
  4. ROS/ROS2 nodes or drivers inside this package: the adapter lives in ros2/pysoarm_ros2 (a separate ament package) and keeps all ROS-independent logic in pysoarm.bridge, which is covered by the main test suite.
  5. Any claim of torque or impedance control on hardware that only has a position loop.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Grow pysoarm into a LeRobot replacement Duplicates an active upstream, inherits its schema churn, and multiplies our dependency and CI surface Bundle a minimal recorder (npz/hdf5, no video) in core Reasonable as a separate package (pysoarm-collect); in core it still adds filesystem/format policy to a driver Add pysoarm[teleop] extra Worth doing only when someone needs teleoperation without LeRobot; the seam is now documented, so it can be added without breaking the layer rule

docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/applebluecode/pysoarm && cd pysoarm
make install-dev     # uv sync --locked + pre-commit hooks
make check           # lint + type + test

Development dependencies are declared as PEP 735 groups in pyproject.toml and pinned by the committed uv.lock, resolved against pypi.org (see [[tool.uv.index]]). Without uv:

python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install --group dev -e .

Only users of the library need pip install pysoarm; nothing in the published metadata depends on the dev groups.

docs.title: Device access
docs.text:
On Linux, add a udev rule so the arms keep stable names across replugs:

scripts/install_udev_rules.sh /dev/ttyACM0 /dev/ttyACM1
# → /dev/so101_follower, /dev/so101_leader

Alternatively make sure your user can open the tty (dialout group, or a 0666 rule).

Also recommended, because it periodically probes serial devices and can make the port momentarily busy:

sudo systemctl disable --now ModemManager

docs.text:
pysoarm --version
pysoarm doctor --port /dev/so101_follower
pysoarm scan   --port /dev/so101_follower   # ids 1..6, model 777 = STS3215

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Version 0.1.1

The snippets below describe the current API and are kept in sync with arm.py.

docs.title: Calibrate a fresh arm
docs.text:
$ pysoarm calibrate --port /dev/ttyACM0 --role follower --id my_follower
$ pysoarm calibration show --port /dev/ttyACM0
$ pysoarm calibration export --port /dev/ttyACM0 --output my_follower.json

The flow disables torque, resets the motor-side calibration, sets half-turn homings (homing_offset = position - 2047), records each joint's travel while you move it, then writes the result back. wrist_roll is recorded over 0..4095 unless --full-turn is used.

docs.title: Leader (read-only) arm
docs.text:
from pysoarm import SOArm

with SOArm("/dev/ttyACM1", role="leader", calibration="my_leader.json") as leader:
    state = leader.read_once()   # no goal is ever written, torque stays off

docs.title: Hold the current pose (safest first program)
docs.text:
from pysoarm import SOArm

with SOArm(port="/dev/so101_follower", calibration="my_follower.json") as arm:
    state = arm.read_once()
    arm.write_goal(state.q_deg)   # goal == measured position: nothing moves
    input("holding — press Enter to release")
# exiting the block disables torque

docs.title: Read telemetry
docs.text:
state = arm.read_once()
print(state.q_deg, state.temperature_c, state.voltage_v, state.t)

docs.title: Smooth move
docs.text: arm.move_to([0, -30, 60, 0, 90, 40], duration=2.0)   # degrees, model joint order

docs.title: Control loop
docs.text:
def policy(state, t):
    return state.q_deg          # returns the goal for the next tick

arm.run_control_loop(policy, hz=200, duration=5.0)

Joint order (both SO-100 and SO-101): shoulder_pan, shoulder_lift, elbow_flex, wrist_flex, wrist_roll, gripper.

docs.title: Reusing an existing LeRobot calibration
docs.text: pysoarm reads LeRobot's JSON format directly (e.g. ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/robots/so_follower/<id>.json), so a calibrated arm does not need to be calibrated again.

docs.title: ROS 2
docs.text:
The ROS 2 integration is a separate package, ros2/pysoarm_ros2, so the device layer keeps zero ROS dependencies (see ADR 0001). It is a thin rclpy node over pysoarm.bridge.ArmBridge, which owns all the logic that can be tested without ROS.

pip install "pysoarm[rustypot]"     # or plain pysoarm
colcon build --packages-select pysoarm_ros2
source install/setup.bash
ros2 run pysoarm_ros2 arm_node --ros-args \
  -p port:=/dev/so101_follower -p backend:=rustypot -p rate_hz:=50.0

docs.text: Direction Name Type Units publish joint_states sensor_msgs/JointState radians (REP 103) subscribe joint_commands std_msgs/Float64MultiArray radians, one per joint service enable std_srvs/Trigger holds the measured pose, enables torque service disable std_srvs/Trigger torque off

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning port /dev/so101_follower serial device model so101 arm model backend scs scs, rustypot or auto calibration "" LeRobot-compatible JSON; empty reads it from the motors rate_hz 50.0 state publish / read rate max_step_deg 5.0 per-tick joint clipping (safety) command_timeout_s 0.25 reject commands based on a state older than this frame_id "" header.frame_id for joint_states

docs.title: Safety behaviour
docs.text:
• every command passes the same guards as the Python API (soft limits, per-step clipping, thermal/supply, watchdog);
  • a rejected command is logged and dropped — it never takes the node down, and the arm keeps its previous goal;
  • a command based on a state older than command_timeout_s is refused, so a stalled loop cannot act on an old reading;
  • disable (or node shutdown) releases torque, and shutdown also closes the serial port.

docs.title: Not covered by CI
docs.text: CI has no ROS installation, so the node itself is only syntax-checked and its module-level tests skip without rclpy. Everything that can be tested without ROS lives in pysoarm.bridge and is covered.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
make check          # lint + type + test (what CI runs)
make lint           # ruff check + ruff format --check
make type           # mypy --strict
make test           # unit tests, no hardware
make cov            # + coverage report
make test-hardware  # PYSOARM_HARDWARE_PORT=/dev/ttyACM0

All targets go through uv run, using the environment pinned in uv.lock (make sync refreshes it; uv sync --locked fails if the lock is stale).

docs.title: Test strategy
docs.text:
• Transport (bus/scs.py, bus/rustypot.py) — covered by protocol-level tests with a fake serial peer, plus opt-in hardware smoke tests.
  • Everything above the transport — runs against FakeBus, including fault injection (fail_next_ops, latency_s, wrong checksum, missing reply). No hardware, no sleeps.
  • Safety guards — pure functions, table-driven tests (clip, clamp, thermal, watchdog).
  • Timing — one hardware test asserts the read+write step stays under 3 ms, so a regression in transaction handling fails CI instead of showing up as jitter in the lab.

filterwarnings = ["error"] is enabled project-wide: a DeprecationWarning from pyserial or a numpy warning is a test failure.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Complete reference for the public API of pysoarm 0.1.0. Every symbol documented here is importable from the top-level package:

from pysoarm import SOArm, ArmState, Calibration, SafetyLimits, Pose

The reference sections are generated from the docstrings by mkdocstrings, so this page and the code cannot drift apart. Start with Conventions and Public API at a glance; task-oriented examples live in the Quickstart.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: The rules below hold across the whole API. Read them once — the rest of the reference assumes them.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Quantity Unit Where Joint positions, goals, limits, step guard degrees SOArm, ArmState.q_deg, Calibration, SafetyLimits Joint positions, ROS bridge input radians only ArmBridge.command_from_radians Cartesian position metres Pose.x/y/z Orientation unit quaternion (w, x, y, z) Pose.qw/qx/qy/qz Euler angles, Pose.angle_to degrees (radians for angle_to) Pose.from_xyz_rpy, Pose.to_xyz_rpy Time, timestamps, durations seconds ArmState.t, duration=, hz= in Hz Temperature, voltage °C, V ArmState.temperature_c, ArmState.voltage_v

Raw servo quantities are not SI and are never silently converted: ArmState.speed_raw and ArmState.current are present_speed / present_current register counts. Use Register.to_unit() when a physical unit matters.

docs.title: Joint order
docs.text:
Every joint tuple and every sequence argument uses the model's joint order, which is the same for SO-100 and SO-101:

Index 0 1 2 3 4 5 Joint shoulder_pan shoulder_lift elbow_flex wrist_flex wrist_roll gripper Motor id 1 2 3 4 5 6

Pass a different RobotModel to change order, ids or count. Sequences that are too short, too long, non-finite, or not in this order raise ConfigurationError before anything is sent to the bus.

docs.title: Values are immutable
docs.text: ArmState, Pose, SafetyReport, JointStateFrame, LoopStats, Register, JointCalibration and RobotModel are frozen dataclasses (JointStateFrame, LoopStats and SafetyReport are plain frozen containers): they are snapshots, never mutated in place. The only stateful objects are SOArm, ArmBridge, the bus transports and Calibration.

docs.title: Nothing is clipped silently
docs.text: SOArm.write_goal() and ArmBridge.command() return the goal that was actually written. Guards clip or derate, and the difference is visible in SafetyReport and in the returned tuple. SOArm.move_to() returns the state measured after the move.

docs.title: Lifetime and threading
docs.text:
SOArm owns its bus: construct it, connect() (or use with), use it, stop(). stop() is idempotent and never raises, so it is safe in a finally block.

from pysoarm import SOArm

with SOArm(port="/dev/so101_follower", calibration="follower.json") as arm:
    arm.hold()
# leaving the block disables torque and closes the port

Instances are not thread-safe: one owner thread per arm. The serial port is exclusive (BusConnectionError if another process holds it). Callbacks passed to SOArm.run_control_loop() run on the loop thread and must not block.

docs.title: Clock and injection seams
docs.text: Construction takes clock= (defaults to time.monotonic), sleep= and — where a dependency is optional — an explicit module seam (placo_module, rustypot_module, serial_factory). Tests use these to run the real code paths with FakeBus and no hardware.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
construct ──► connect() ──► read_once()/write_goal()/move_to() ──► stop()
              │             └── run_control_loop() (owns the loop)
              └── open bus → configure motors (torque off) → hold measured pose → torque on

connect() is deliberately conservative: torque stays off while the motors are configured, the measured pose is written back as the first goal, and only then is torque enabled — the arm cannot jump on connect. The steps are idempotent where possible; calling connect() twice is harmless, and stop() may be called at any time in any state.

docs.title: Typical calls
docs.text:
from pysoarm import SOArm

arm = SOArm(port="/dev/so101_follower", calibration="follower.json")
arm.connect()

state = arm.read_once()          # q_deg, temperature_c, voltage_v, t, ...
arm.hold()                       # re-read and command the measured pose

goal = arm.write_goal([0, -30, 60, 0, 90, 40])   # returns what was written
arm.move_to([0, -20, 60, 0, 90, 40], duration=2.0, profile="minjerk")

def policy(state, elapsed_s):
    return state.q_deg           # None means "hold, send nothing"

stats = arm.run_control_loop(policy, hz=200, duration=5.0)
print(stats.ticks, stats.overruns)
arm.stop()

docs.title: Reading states
docs.text:
health= Registers refreshed Transactions per tick False none (cache reused) 1 sync read — the hot path True all health registers 1 sync read + 1 read None (default) one health register per tick, round-robin, once the cache is older than health_period_s 1 sync read (+1 periodically)

That amortisation is what keeps a 200 Hz loop inside its 5 ms budget while temperature and voltage stay fresh enough for the guards.

docs.title: pysoarm.arm
docs.text:
SOArm — the high-level device object.

Shaped after pylibfranka.Robot / pyAgxArm so calling code reads the same way, within what position-servo hardware allows::

with SOArm(port="/dev/so101_follower", calibration="follower.json") as arm:
    state = arm.read_once()
    arm.move_to([0, -30, 60, 0, 90, 40], duration=2.0)
    arm.run_control_loop(lambda s, t: policy(s), hz=200, duration=5.0)

Design rules:

  • hold before you move — connect() reads the measured pose and writes it back as the first goal, so the first command can never be a jump;
  • clipping is observable — write_goal() returns the goal actually sent, never silently reduced;
  • one sync read + one sync write per control tick — health registers are cached and refreshed every health_period_s instead of on every tick;
  • stop() is idempotent and safe from finally/signal handlers — it disables torque then closes the bus, in that order.

docs.title: LoopStats dataclass
docs.text:
LoopStats(
    ticks,
    overruns,
    elapsed_s,
    errors=0,
    consecutive_errors_max=0,
    latencies_s=(),
)

Summary of a finished control loop.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ticks int

Number of completed ticks (including ticks that ended in a handled error).

required overruns int

Ticks that could not be finished within the period. This is also the number of missed deadlines: the loop keeps absolute deadlines, so a missed tick is counted rather than hidden by shortening the next period.

required elapsed_s float

Wall-clock duration of the loop.

required errors int

Ticks that raised and were handled by a non-abort error policy.

0 consecutive_errors_max int

Longest run of consecutive failed ticks.

0 latencies_s tuple[float, ...]

Per-tick command latency, measured from the callback's sampling instant to the completed goal write. Only ticks that wrote a goal are recorded.

()

All derived values are computed on demand, so the object stays a cheap immutable record.

docs.title: Calibration: pysoarm.calibration
docs.text:
Calibration maps raw ticks to degrees and defines each joint's usable travel. It comes from one of three places:

  1. a Calibration object you build,
  2. a LeRobot JSON file (.from_lerobot(path) / to_lerobot(path) — pysoarm reads LeRobot's format directly, so a calibrated arm does not need calibrating again),
  3. the motors themselves (calibration=None at construction reads the stored calibration).

validate(model) is called by connect(): missing joints, extra joints or duplicated motor ids raise CalibrationError before any motor is commanded.

The motor-side flow is public in pysoarm.calibration:

Function Purpose read_calibration(bus, model) read limits + homing offsets from the servos write_calibration(bus, model, cal) persist a calibration to the servos reset_calibration(bus, model) clear offsets, widen travel to 0..4095 set_half_turn_homings(bus, model) Feetech offset = position - 2047 record_ranges(bus, model, stop=...) poll travel while the operator moves the arm calibrate(bus, model, role=..., full_turn=...) the full flow above

docs.title: pysoarm.calibration
docs.text:
Calibration: homing offsets, joint ranges and the degrees <-> tick conversion.

The on-disk format is intentionally LeRobot-compatible, so an arm that was already calibrated by LeRobot can be driven by pysoarm without re-calibration::

{
  "shoulder_pan": {"id": 1, "drive_mode": 0, "homing_offset": -1902,
                   "range_min": 732, "range_max": 3380},
  ...
}

Conversions (the STS3215 has 4096 ticks per turn, so 4095 is the largest representable raw value)::

raw   = round(q_deg * 4095 / 360 + (range_min + range_max) / 2)
q_deg = (raw - (range_min + range_max) / 2) * 360 / 4095

drive_mode == 1 marks a mirrored mounting: the sign is flipped in both directions. LeRobot ignores drive_mode in degrees mode; pysoarm applies it, because a mirrored joint that is not flipped moves the wrong way. All SO-101 factory calibrations use drive_mode = 0.

docs.title: Safety: pysoarm.safety
docs.text:
Every goal passes the same guard chain in write_goal() — there is no bypass flag:

Order Guard Threshold On trip 1 Finiteness — SafetyViolation 2 Watchdog max_consecutive_failures WatchdogTimeout (torque already off) 3 Temperature temp_max_c SafetyViolation 4 Voltage voltage_min_v SafetyViolation 5 Calibrated limits limit_margin_deg goal clamped inward, clipped=True 6 Step size max_step_deg (scaled by the derate factor) goal clipped to state.q_deg ± max_step 7 Derating temp_warn_c SafetyLimits.derate() returns a factor in (0.25, 1.0] from the hottest motor, which shrinks the allowed step

SafetyLimits() defaults are the reference values used on the reference arm:

Field Default Meaning max_step_deg 5.0 Largest change of a joint between two goals limit_margin_deg 1.0 Margin kept inside the calibrated travel temp_warn_c 55.0 Above this, goals are derated temp_max_c 70.0 At this, goals are refused voltage_min_v 10.0 Below this, goals are refused max_consecutive_failures 3 Read failures before the watchdog trips

The contract on tripping is part of the API: WatchdogTimeout leaves torque off, and SafetyViolation/CalibrationError/NotReachableError are raised before a goal is written, so the arm keeps its last safe target. Temperature is judged on the hottest motor (ArmState.max_temperature_c) and voltage on the lowest one (ArmState.min_voltage_v).

docs.title: pysoarm.safety
docs.text:
Safety guards applied to every goal before it reaches the bus.

Guards are pure functions of the requested goal, the current state and the limits, so all the rules are unit-testable without hardware. They run in this order:

  1. validity — correct joint count, finite values, known joints (ConfigurationError);
  2. watchdog — too many consecutive read failures (WatchdogTimeout);
  3. thermal / supply — too hot or undervoltage (SafetyViolation);
  4. soft limits — clamp to the calibrated travel minus a margin;
  5. per-step clipping — |q_goal - q_now| <= max_step_deg * derate, the guard that makes the first goal after connect (and every goal after a lost frame) unable to cause a jump.

A small, framework-agnostic bridge for exposing an arm to another process.

docs.title: pysoarm.bus.base
docs.text:
The Bus protocol: the only boundary the control code is allowed to cross.

Above this boundary nothing imports serial or rustypot and everything is expressed in raw register values; below it nothing knows about degrees, calibration or limits. That split is what lets the whole control path run against :class:~pysoarm.bus.fake.FakeBus in tests.

Implementations must honour these rules:

  • one batch call per control step — call sync_read/sync_write instead of looping in application code. On this hardware sync_read is internally sequential (the TTL bus is half-duplex), but keeping it a single call is what makes swapping in a faster backend or a fake painless;
  • retries are idempotent — a retry must not change the value written;
  • raise, do not block — a missing reply becomes :class:~pysoarm.exceptions.CommunicationError after the configured retries, with the raw bytes attached for post-mortem;
  • stateless — no calibration, no unit conversion, no clipping. Those live above.

docs.title: pysoarm.bus.scs
docs.text:
SCS protocol over pyserial — the reference backend and the only hard dependency.

Wire format (Feetech SCS/STS, 8N1, 1 Mbaud)::

request   FF FF  ID  LEN  INSTR  [PARAMS...]  CHECKSUM
response  FF FF  ID  LEN  ERROR  [DATA...]    CHECKSUM

with LEN = len(PARAMS) + 2 (a two-byte READ therefore uses LEN = 4 — the value most easily got wrong), CHECKSUM = ~(ID + LEN + INSTR + PARAMS) & 0xFF and broadcast id 0xFE. Instructions used here: PING 0x01, READ 0x02, WRITE 0x03, SYNC_WRITE 0x83.

The bus is half-duplex: while the host transmits, a servo's reply cannot be on the wire. Pipelining requests (sending all six before reading any reply) therefore corrupts the stream on real hardware — measured, and the reason :meth:ScsBus.sync_read issues one request/response pair per servo and collects them into one mapping. Broadcast SYNC_WRITE is the exception: the host is the only transmitter, so six goals go out in a single frame.

Measured on the reference hardware (six joints, 1 Mbaud, this backend): single register read 0.30 ms, six-joint sync_read ~1.8 ms (sequential pairs), six-goal sync_write 0.26 ms. A Rust driver (rustypot) pipelines at a lower level and reaches ~1 ms; this module trades that for zero non-Python dependencies.

docs.title: pysoarm.bus.rustypot
docs.text:
Optional rustypot backend: the same bus, driven from Rust.

rustypot is the driver LeRobot uses for the STS3215. It speaks the same SCS protocol but does the request/response bookkeeping in Rust, so a six-joint read costs ~1 ms instead of the ~2.2 ms the pure-Python :class:~pysoarm.bus.scs.ScsBus needs. It is an optional extra::

pip install "pysoarm[rustypot]"

Select it explicitly — SOArm(..., backend="rustypot"), pysoarm scan --backend rustypot — or pass backend="auto" to use it when it is importable and fall back to scs otherwise.

Notes on the mapping:

  • rustypot does not reject writes to read-only registers, so this adapter checks :data:~pysoarm.bus.registers.REGISTERS first (same behaviour as ScsBus);
  • rustypot raises ValueError for a bad id/register name, RuntimeError for a bus failure and OSError when the port cannot be opened; these are translated to :class:~pysoarm.exceptions.ConfigurationError, CommunicationError and BusConnectionError respectively;
  • the port is opened with an exclusive lock, so a second process fails loudly.

Deterministic in-memory bus for tests and offline development.

The fake keeps a register map per motor, moves present_position to goal_position when a goal is written (instant tracking, torque on), and records every transaction in :attr:FakeBus.calls so tests can assert that the control loop issues exactly one sync read and one sync write per tick — never a per-joint loop.

docs.text:
SO-101 / SO-100 description.

Six STS3215 servos, ids 1-6, in this order (the order every array in this package uses)::

shoulder_pan  shoulder_lift  elbow_flex  wrist_flex  wrist_roll  gripper

SO-100 shares the bus layout; only the mechanics differ, so it is registered as an alias with its own name. LeRobot's follower and leader use the same layout — the leader has no torque and is read-only from this package's point of view.

docs.title: Kinematics: pysoarm.kinematics
docs.text:
Kinematics is optional and out of the control loop: the position loop works in joint space, and kinematics only converts to and from Cartesian goals. A SO-101 URDF is not shipped (licensing and the accuracy of community meshes vary) — pass your own.

from pysoarm import SOArm
from pysoarm.kinematics import PlacoKinematics

arm = SOArm(
    port="/dev/so101_follower",
    calibration="follower.json",
    kinematics=PlacoKinematics("so101.urdf", target_frame="gripper_frame_link"),
)
with arm:
    pose = arm.forward()                     # FK of the current joints
    arm.move_to_pose(pose, duration=2.0)     # IK, then a joint-space move

import pysoarm stays dependency-free: the placo adapter is imported lazily on first use, and a missing dependency raises KinematicsError with the install command. move_to_pose() solves IK before writing any goal, so an unreachable target raises NotReachableError and leaves the arm where it was.

docs.title: pysoarm.kinematics.placo_solver
docs.text:
Inverse/forward kinematics through placo (optional extra).

placo builds a kinematic model from a URDF and solves frame tasks with a damped least-squares step. The adapters here:

  • work in degrees and metres at the boundary (radians internally, as placo expects);
  • use a small task gain (1e-3) and iterate until the position residual is below tolerance_m — a gain of 1.0 overshoots and lands in a wrong branch on the reference two-link model, so the default is deliberately conservative;
  • seed the solver from the current joint configuration (a Cartesian move from the current pose converges in a handful of iterations);
  • raise :class:~pysoarm.exceptions.NotReachableError with the residual instead of returning a saturated joint vector.

Orientation is not constrained by default (orientation_gain=0): a 4-DoF arm cannot meet a full 6-D pose, and silently trading position against orientation is worse than ignoring it. Set orientation_gain on arms with enough degrees of freedom.

docs.text:
pysoarm CLI entry point.

Sub-commands::

pysoarm scan    --port /dev/so101_follower      # ids + model numbers on the bus
pysoarm read    --port ... --json               # one snapshot, machine readable
pysoarm monitor --port ... --hz 5               # live positions/temps/voltages
pysoarm hold    --port ... --yes                # enable torque, hold the current pose
pysoarm calibrate --port ... --role follower    # motor-side calibration flow
pysoarm calibration show --port ...             # print the calibration stored in the motors
pysoarm calibration export --port ... --output f.json
pysoarm bench   --port ... --seconds 5          # read/write latency and loop overruns
pysoarm doctor  --port ... [--stress 3]         # environment + electrical self-check

doctor exists because the two most common failures are environmental: another process (a suspended lerobot-*) holding the tty, and ModemManager probing /dev/ttyACM*. With --stress it also reports per-motor timeouts, status bits and voltage/temperature.

docs.title: Exceptions: pysoarm.exceptions
docs.text:
Every error derives from PysoarmError, so one except can catch this package without swallowing unrelated OSError/ValueError:

PysoarmError
├── ConfigurationError        bad arguments, unknown joint/register, bad calibration
├── BusConnectionError        port unavailable or held by another process
├── CommunicationError        no reply / corrupt packet; arm holds its last goal
│                             (.motor_id, .register, .raw)
├── CalibrationError          calibration missing, incomplete or mismatched
├── SafetyViolation           non-finite goal, over-temperature, undervoltage
│   └── WatchdogTimeout       too many consecutive read failures; torque is off
└── KinematicsError           kinematics unavailable or failed
    └── NotReachableError     IK did not converge; no goal was written

The recovery contract is part of the type: WatchdogTimeout means torque is already off, and the errors raised during a move mean no goal was written, so a try/except around a move leaves the arm in a defined state.

docs.title: pysoarm.exceptions

Exception hierarchy.

Every error raised by this package derives from :class:PysoarmError, so callers can catch one type without swallowing unrelated failures (OSError from pyserial, ValueError from user code, ...).

Physical safety is treated as part of the contract: :class:WatchdogTimeout and :class:SafetyViolation must leave the arm in a defined state (torque off or last safe goal), and that is stated in their docstrings.

CommunicationError(
    message,
    *,
    motor_id=None,
    register=None,
    raw=None,
    status=None,
    transient=True,
    attempts=1,

A motor did not answer, or answered with a corrupt/error status packet.

The arm is left holding its last goal; the caller (or the watchdog) decides whether to keep going. The structured fields make that decision mechanical instead of textual::

try:
    bus.sync_read(ids, "present_position")
except CommunicationError as exc:
    if exc.transient and exc.attempts < 5:
        ...  # retry the whole transaction

Name Type Description motor_id

Motor that failed, when known.

register

Register name involved, when known.

raw

Raw bytes received (or sent), for post-mortem; None if nothing arrived.

status

The SCS/STS ERROR byte, or None when the failure was not a status packet (timeout, checksum, wrong id, short payload).

transient

Whether repeating the identical, idempotent transaction may succeed. No-reply, checksum, truncated frames and servo alarm bits are transient; a mis-addressed or malformed request is not (that is a ConfigurationError).

Number of attempts actually made, including the failed one.

docs.title: NotReachableError
docs.text:
Bases: KinematicsError

Inverse kinematics did not converge to the requested pose.

Raised before any goal is written, so the arm keeps its current target. The residual distance is included in the message.

docs.title: SafetyViolation
docs.text:
Bases: PysoarmError

A guard rejected a goal because executing it would be unsafe.

The arm keeps its previous goal; no new goal is written.

docs.title: WatchdogTimeout
docs.text:
Bases: SafetyViolation

Bus communication was lost for longer than the watchdog allows.

The caller must disable torque (SOArm does so before re-raising) — a servo holding a stale goal while the host believes it is communicating is exactly the failure mode this guard exists for.
